analysis.one_liner: Extended the federal ban on evicting renters behind on rent during the pandemic through the end of 2021.
analysis.headline: The bill to extend the CDC eviction moratorium through the end of 2021 died in committee without ever getting a House vote, days after the Supreme Court blocked the moratorium's further extension.
analysis.plain_summary: In the summer of 2021, a federal ban on evicting renters who couldn't pay because of the pandemic was about to end. This bill would have extended that ban through December 31, 2021, keeping families in their homes while emergency rental aid caught up. It was referred to a House committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters behind on rent during the pandemic, who could not have been evicted for nonpayment through December 31, 2021, and their families and communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters behind on rent during the pandemic

how_it_helps.text: It extended the CDC order halting most residential evictions through December 31, 2021, so renters behind on rent during the pandemic could not be removed from their homes for nonpayment during that period.
By codifying the moratorium in statute, it aimed to keep the protection alive even after the Supreme Court ruled that the CDC lacked authority to extend it on its own.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords, who would have carried unpaid rent for the extension period; the federal government was separately distributing emergency rental assistance to cover some of those arrears.

drawbacks.text: Extending the moratorium shifted the cost to landlords, including small landlords who receive no rent while still owing mortgages, taxes, and maintenance.
A blanket extension through December 31 was broad, and by late summer 2021 the public-health rationale was weakening as vaccines became widely available.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a straightforward, time-limited protection during a public-health emergency at a real cost to landlords, some of them small operators facing their own mortgage bills; a fair process would have weighed a targeted extension (with hardship requirements already in the CDC order) rather than letting it die without any vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House committee the day it was introduced and never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended; a same-day attempt to bring it straight to the floor was blocked by a single objection.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2021 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee two days later.
On July 30, House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer tried to bring the bill straight to the floor by unanimous consent with an amendment, but a single member's objection blocked it.
No further action was ever taken, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without a vote in either chamber.

The bill's purpose was overtaken in part by the Supreme Court's August 2021 decision in Alabama Association of Realtors v. HHS, which held the CDC lacked legal authority to keep the eviction moratorium in place, ending the protection the bill sought to revive.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and the apartment industry, who regained the ability to evict nonpaying tenants once the moratorium lapsed; renters behind on rent lost the protection without Congress ever voting on it.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the CDC eviction moratorium through December 31, 2021.

for.name: Steny Hoyer
for.what_they_did: Asked unanimous consent to discharge the Energy and Commerce Committee and bring the bill to the floor with an amendment; the request failed when objection was heard.

against.name: Unidentified objecting member(s) of the House
against.what_they_did: Objected when Leader Hoyer asked unanimous consent to discharge the committee and take up the bill, killing that path the day after introduction.

against.name: National Association of Realtors and apartment industry groups
against.role: Landlord and real estate industry organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed extension of the federal eviction moratorium and backed the court challenge that led the Supreme Court to strike it down.

sides.party_line_note: All 102 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill also died through the House's objection-based floor process without a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from evicting nonpaying tenants through the end of 2021, forcing them to absorb the cost. Its failure, together with the Supreme Court ruling, restored their ability to evict.

industries.industry: Real estate and apartment industry groups
industries.note: The National Apartment Association and similar groups opposed extending the federal moratorium, and its defeat preserved their members' ability to recover unpaid rent and regain units.
